thread.title: Sand In My Shoes - Why I Bought PPL - PPL Corporation (NYSE:PPL)

author: Brian Soule
title: Sand In My Shoes - Why I Bought PPL - PPL Corporation (NYSE:PPL)
text:
PPL Corp. ( PPL ), formerly Pennsylvania Power & Light, was founded in Allentown PA in 1920. Today, in addition to having regulated electricity distribution in Pennsylvania, they also are doing business in Kentucky (both gas and electric) and the United Kingdom. Yes, really. Actually, over 50% of PPL's earnings come from their UK subsidiary.
Never have I ever considered looking at this "Dividend Contender" (as classified by the late, great David Fish ), but I ran a sort of different screen, one I never would have considered doing until I started tracking my dividend payouts graphically.
If you look at the dividend report from my latest monthly update , you will notice that every January, April, July, and October my dividends are somewhat lacking (see my graph from that article below).
I don't need them to be perfectly even. When the fetching Mrs. Soule and I eventually hang up our laptop carrying cases and corporate ID badges, we will be smart enough to know that if we are getting $9,000 worth of dividends in August but only $2,800 in October that we should probably not spend the entire $9,000 in the month that we get it.
Chart created by author using actual dividend data from my portfolio
But, in an effort to smooth out the chart at least a little bit, I ran a screen on David Fish's "U.S. Dividend Champions" spreadsheet for CCC stocks that pay a dividend in the months where I'm a little light. Of course, some old familiar names turned up like Illinois Tool Works ( ITW ) and Genuine Parts Co. ( GPC ) which I already own and I considered adding to those. Some other names that I've been following also turned up like Kimberly-Clark Corp. ( KMB ), the Coca-Cola Company ( KO ), and Cardinal Health Inc. ( CAH ), but none of them seemed to be at the levels I wanted to add.
I also considered adding another REIT, and there were literally dozens of names to choose from but with the two fairly large positions I already have in that sector I passed.
This led me to a name I had never before considered, that of PPL. So other than the timing of their dividend payout, what, you might ask, are the other reasons I purchased the stock?
Dividend Yield One of the other attractions to me was the very juicy dividend yield. At the time of this writing, the yield stood at 5.33% which is well above my portfolio's historical yield of 3.5-3.7% and would be a welcome addition. Not to mention, if you look at the below chart, you can see that the yield is considerably above the 4-year average yield of 4.52%.
PPL Dividend Yield (TTM) data by YCharts
High ROE I recently purchased Consolidated Edison Inc. (NYSE: ED ) in part because of their fairly high and fairly steady ROE. As you can see below, PPL's ROE is not as steady as Con Ed's, not close, but the average is certainly higher. Going back to 2008, the average ROE of PPL is somewhere north of 12% while ED is remarkably steady but does not get close to 12% anywhere over the last five years.
We will see why this is important in a little bit.
PPL Return on Equity (TTM) data by YCharts
Capital Plan Should Stimulate Growth PPL is, like my recent purchase of Exxon Mobil Corp. ( XOM ), planning to spend a lot of dough in the near future on capital projects to increase future earnings. From 2018-2022, PPL expects to invest $15 billion in infrastructure projects and mostly because of this Morningstar (subscription required) projects a 5.5% annual earnings growth.
Morningstar's analysis aligns with PPL's own statement:
Looking ahead, we expect at least 5 to 6 percent annual earnings per share growth from 2018 through 2020 off of our 2018 forecast midpoint of $2.30 per share.
Source: PPL 2017 Annual Report
$15 billion in capital spending over five years is about $3 billion per year. There is only one problem with this scenario and that is PPL's operating cash flow is usually not $3 billion. In fact, only once over the past five years did it exceed $3B, and that was back in 2014.
So that means that free cash flow is usually negative. I don't like that. And what are they doing to raise the cash? Well, they are issuing both equity and debt to make up the shortfall.
So, shares are not being repurchased, and I am generally pro-share repurchases. Also, they are not reducing their outstanding debt, in fact, they are adding to their debt load, and I am generally against companies being heavily leveraged.
But, let's remember that PPL has an ROE well above 12% on average. The return they earn on their investments far exceed the costs of raising the capital needed for that investment. When a company continues to generate excess returns on their capital raised, the company will almost certainly increase in value as their growth increases. This part I like.
Show Me the Money PPL is a dividend contender, having raised their dividend for 17 consecutive years. Their yield as of this writing was 5.3% and the 5-year growth rate of the dividend has been 3.1% (data from the DRiP Investing Resource Center ).
The low DGR is offset by the high starting yield. However, Morningstar projects a 4% dividend growth rate over the next 5 years given the aggressive capital plan I mentioned above.
Dividend Discount Model Since the very first reason I gave for purchasing this stock was the nice dividend, I thought it was wise to run a dividend discount model, which takes the present value of all future projected dividends and sums them up. (I never thought I'd use this in "real life" when I was in college, yet here we are).
I've run this model several times already for other steady dividend-paying stocks, but in case you missed them or have never seen the model before, here is the formula for the dividend discount model:
Price per share = D/(r - g)
Where:
D = the Dividend (yearly) of the stock
r = the cost of capital, sometimes called Weighted Average Cost of Capital or WACC
g = the growth of the dividend, in perpetuity
The easiest of these three variables to find is the current yearly dividend, or "D". In this case, it is $1.64 per share.
The cost of capital is a little bit tougher, and while there are ways to calculate this on your own, I generally defer to the "big guys" and go with their assumptions. However, in this case, the big guys are all over the map. I have seen numbers as low as 4.1% and numbers much higher, upwards of 9% and above. When your dividend is 5.3%, it seems to me that your cost of equity is at least that. Even Morningstar suggests the cost of equity is 7.5%, while their estimate for the WACC is lower.
We use a 7.5% cost of equity and a 6.2% weighted average cost of capital in our discounted cash flow valuation.
Not sure about you, but 7% sounds about right to me, maybe even a little higher.
As far as the growth of the dividend, I already mentioned that Morningstar estimates a 4% dividend growth rate, and that more or less checks out with the recent past. Most recently, the dividend was raised from $0.395 per quarter to $0.41, a 3.8% increase. Even still, with the power of spreadsheets, I will run a few different scenarios, the results can be seen in the table below:
D 1.64 1.64 1.64 1.64 1.64 1.64 r 7% 8% 9% 7% 8% 9% g 4.0% 4.0% 4.0% 3.5% 3.5% 3.5% P 54.67 41.00 32.80 46.86 36.44 29.82 Table created by the author, dividend data from Seeking Alpha, WACC and dividend growth rate are assumptions
The price, as you may or may not know, of PPL was just below $31 per share at the time of this writing. As you can see, the only scenario where the dividend discount model gives us a price lower than that was with a 3.5% dividend growth rate and a 9% cost of capital. At a 7% WACC, the stock is wildly undervalued at $31 per share (according to this model). At a 6.2% WACC, which Morningstar uses, the price is even more ridiculous.
For the sake of completeness, Morningstar gives PPL a "fair value estimate" of $35 and their "consider buy" number is $28.
Objections: So, what might have kept me from buying this stock (but didn't)?
Well, for starters, I do not like to buy stocks of companies with large and growing debt. PPL's debt is certainly growing and will continue to do so it would appear given their capital plans, but the debt to equity ratio for the trailing twelve months (ttm) is 1.69 according to Morningstar.
That is better than Southern Company ( SO ), one of the utilities I currently own and not as good as the other one ( ED ). So that is not so bad. Not ideal, but not bad.
Their free cash flow is not flowing. In fact, it is negative. I love, and I mean LOVE, companies that generate gobs and gobs of free cash. This is not one of them and that was a tough hurdle for me to get over. Usually, one of the first things I do when researching a company is skip right past the income statement and balance sheet and go right to the cash flow statement and then go right to the bottom of that and look up the free cash flow. I did that here also but remembered that utilities generally do not have the kind of free cash flow that a company like Apple Inc. ( AAPL ) or Cisco Systems Inc. ( CSCO ) has. Primarily because the capital required to generate a dollar of sales for AAPL is so, so much lower than it is for a utility.
Since over half of PPL's earnings come from the UK, the risk of foreign currency exchange can sometimes slam this stock, which allowed me to buy when I did where I did. The day I bought PPL (Nov. 15), the stock was down 5.2% from the previous day. It just so happens that Teresa May was getting grilled about her "Brexit" plans in front of Parliament that same day. While that could be a concern, it should also be noted that PPL understands this too and does hedge against this risk. Am I worried? Not really. I would see any future panic about Brexit as another buying opportunity.
The final concern is that the aggressive capital plan could limit dividend growth. You might figure that as more and more shares are issued the expense of the dividend grows and the company would slow down or eliminate future dividend increases. Likewise, issuing more debt will only increase the interest expense in the future and that would suck up more cash that could be used to pay a higher dividend. However, we must keep in mind that as long as the ROE remains higher than the cost of capital, the earnings should continue to grow, and the dividends should grow at a modest rate right along with them.
Final Thoughts So, on November 15, I purchased 75 shares of PPL for $30.51 per share. The primary purpose of this position was to add a hefty dividend to the months of January, April, July, and October and this accomplishes that. I added $30+ per quarter to my dividend income which is very nice.
A day after my purchase they announced their next dividend, and the stock goes ex on December 7th, payable January 2. Also, this should be the final dividend at the current rate of $0.41 per share and I would expect the dividend to be raised to perhaps $0.425 per share at their next announcement.
I will be keeping an eye on their capital spending and making sure that their revenues and earnings are rising along with or faster than their debt levels. This is key for the dividend increases I expect. If the pace of dividend growth slows considerably or stops I will, of course, re-evaluate this position at that time.
In the meantime, however, I will be quite happy to sit back and receive my 5.3% yield, and I am looking forward already to the next dividend increase which I expect will be announced sometime in February.
As always, thank you for reading this and best of luck to you and yours this holiday season.
Disclosure: I am/we are long AAPL, CSCO, ED, GPC, ITW, PPL, SO, XOM.
